description: Knechtle argues that God provides sufficient intellectual and affective evidence for freely chosen trust, whereas undeniable manifestation would secure only assent, not relationship.
critique: Strongest feature: Knechtle directly confronts Dillahunty’s communicative-God challenge by distinguishing propositional assent from voluntarily relational trust, while Matthew 28 suggests physical encounter need not produce enduring belief. Principal limitation: Neither the claim that resurrection witnesses soon abandoned belief nor “just enough evidence” establishes an assessable threshold; moreover, clearer disclosure is characterized as coercive without addressing intermediate possibilities or nonresistant uncertainty. Live burden: Knechtle must demonstrate that Christianity’s intellectual and affective indicators are sufficient, explain why stronger yet resistible evidence would damage freely chosen relationship, and connect his disciples comparison to divine hiddenness. Locked score: 70 rewards direct engagement and substantial motion-level relevance, while weak evidential grounding, undefined calibration, and incomplete contact with Dillahunty’s objection keep this coherent distinction from establishing Christianity’s rationality.
